about: Which side each share value belongs to (bears, neutral or bulls), with the multiple, the market mood that would take the price there, and why. UI/pipeline/share_values.py reads this file, so the same link applies to every asset. It is written for review by an expert: change a side, a multiple or a reason here, and every asset's next update uses it.

sides.bears: The pessimistic case: a low valuation, the kind bears argue for in a sell-off.
sides.neutral: An ordinary market: the shares valued at market or sector norms.
sides.bulls: The optimistic case: a high valuation, the kind bulls argue for in a rally.

fundamentals.net_cash: Cash and short-term investments minus all debt, at the end of the last quarter, per share.
fundamentals.tangible_book: Shareholders' equity minus goodwill and other intangible assets, at the end of the last quarter, per share.
fundamentals.book: Shareholders' equity at the end of the last quarter, per share.
fundamentals.revenue: Revenue over the last four quarters, per share.
fundamentals.revenue_pace: Revenue of the last quarter times four, per share.
fundamentals.earnings: Net income to common shareholders over the last four quarters, per share.
fundamentals.ebitda: EBITDA without one-off items over the last four quarters, per share. Its value is the enterprise value (EBITDA times the multiple) minus net debt.
fundamentals.fcf: Free cash flow (operating cash flow minus capital spending) over the last four quarters, per share.

values.sentiment: Capitulation: only the cash left after paying all debt counts
values.why: Gives the business itself no value: only cash net of every debt remains. It is the liquidation floor bears point to in a panic.

values.sentiment: Crash: priced at its tangible assets alone
values.why: Counts only tangible net assets, treats goodwill and intangibles as worthless and adds nothing for earning power: a distressed-sale view.

values.sentiment: Deep pessimism: priced at book value, as in a sell-off
values.why: A price-to-book of 1 says the business is worth only its accounting net assets, far below the market's usual 3 to 5 times book: the classic bear floor.

values.sentiment: Pessimism: each dollar of yearly revenue priced at a dollar
values.why: One times revenue is below the S&P 500's long-run price-to-sales of about 1.5 to 2 and well below its recent level near 3: priced like a low-margin or shrinking business.

values.sentiment: An ordinary market: revenue valued near the S&P 500's recent multiple
values.why: About three times revenue is where the S&P 500 as a whole has traded in recent years: neither a discount nor a premium.

values.sentiment: Growth enthusiasm: the newest quarter's pace, at a growth-stock multiple
values.why: Two optimistic choices at once: the latest quarter's revenue annualized, as if growth holds, and a price-to-sales of 10, which only fast growers command.

values.sentiment: Pessimism: earnings priced like a value stock
values.why: A P/E of 12 is below the S&P 500's long-run average of about 16 and its recent 20 to 25: the multiple of a stock the market expects little from.

values.sentiment: An ordinary market: earnings valued like the S&P 500 today
values.why: The S&P 500's own trailing P/E today, live from Yahoo (SPY): the average stock's multiple, neutral by definition.

values.sentiment: In step with its sector: earnings valued like its sector today
values.why: The trailing P/E of the asset's sector ETF today (its comparison series), live from Yahoo: valued like its peers, no better and no worse.

values.sentiment: Optimism: a growth premium on earnings
values.why: A P/E of 35 is well above the market's: investors pay it only when they expect earnings to grow fast for years.

values.sentiment: Pessimism: operating earnings at a low multiple
values.why: An enterprise value of 8 times EBITDA is below the market's usual 12 to 16: priced like a mature or troubled business.

values.sentiment: An ordinary market: operating earnings at a typical multiple
values.why: About 14 times EBITDA is close to the S&P 500's average in recent years, around 12 to 16.

values.sentiment: Optimism: operating earnings at a growth multiple
values.why: 25 times EBITDA is a growth-company multiple, paid when investors expect operating earnings to rise fast.

values.sentiment: Pessimism: free cash flow priced to yield about 8%
values.why: 12 times free cash flow is a free-cash-flow yield of about 8%, roughly double the market's: the price of a stock investors distrust.

values.sentiment: An ordinary market: free cash flow priced to yield about 4.5%
values.why: 22 times free cash flow, a yield of about 4.5%, is close to the market's long-run free-cash-flow yield of 4 to 5%.

values.sentiment: Optimism: free cash flow priced to yield 2.5%, paying for growth
values.why: 40 times free cash flow, a 2.5% yield, makes sense only if the cash flow is expected to grow fast.
